opening.headline: Learn how to divide code scoring and model scoring when human scoring is slow and inconsistent.
body: When the evaluation set grows to hundreds or thousands of evaluations, it becomes difficult for people to read and grade them one by one. Different raters give different values ​​to the same answer, and even the same person's standards change over time. Each time you change the prompt or model, you have to re-score from the beginning, which is expensive.

In this class, we will compare the pros and cons of code grading, human grading, and model grading, and check the differences by grading the same answer with code and model. Next, we look at examples of how to use a scoring rubric and how to check for bias in model scoring.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the pros and cons of code scoring and model scoring
Grading methods can be categorized by assignment type.

screens.title: Human grading is slow and inconsistent
screens.lead: Read about teams that have grown in scale. It's good to read while thinking about where human grading encounters its limitations.

paragraphs: One team grew its evaluation set from hundreds to thousands. Then the idea of ​​having people reading and grading the responses one by one started to get overwhelming. Grading took several days, so each time I changed the prompt I had to wait that long to see the results.

The bigger issue is consistency. Different raters give different values ​​to the same answer, and even the same person has different standards in the morning and afternoon. You want to know which change worked, but you can't tell whether the difference in values ​​is due to the change or grading fluctuations.

So a fast and consistent grading method is needed. Scoring methods are largely divided into methods where rules are checked with code, methods where a person reads and judges, and methods where a model reads and judges. This class compares these three and establishes a standard for selecting the appropriate one for each task.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The purpose of the evaluation is to reliably measure the difference before and after the change. If the grading method is shaky, you won't be able to trust the difference.

screens.outro: First, let's think about the differences in grading standards you've encountered.

screens.title: Think back: An experience where grading criteria were different for each person.
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about your experience first and then click on it.

items.prompt: Have you ever had an experience where the grading criteria were different for each person? On what topic did opinions differ?
items.answer: It is common for opinions to differ on items such as accuracy, tone, and length. Divided opinions are often a sign that standards exist only in people's heads and not in writing.

items.prompt: Have you written down those criteria?
items.answer: If you write down the standards, you will be able to judge them by looking at the same sentence, which increases the level of agreement. The criteria written in this article are the grading rubrics that will be discussed later.

items.prompt: Can a machine follow the standards you write down?
items.answer: If the rules are clear, the code can follow them, and for judgments that are difficult to write down as rules, the model can read the rubric and follow them. Which one is right for you will depend on the nature of the task.

screens.outro: Let’s start by comparing the pros and cons of the three grading methods.

screens.title: Pros and cons of three grading methods
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the speed, reliability, and flexibility of each scoring method.

tabs.label: Code grading
tabs.body: This is a method of judgment based on rules and codes. It is the fastest, most reliable and can be run at scale. On the other hand, it is weak in subtle judgments that cannot be contained in rules. Typical examples include exact matches, which check whether the output is exactly the same as the correct answer, string inclusion checks, which check whether key phrases are included in the output, and checks that compare structured field values.

tabs.label: human grading
tabs.body: This is how people read and judge. The most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive. So, avoid it if possible and use it only where absolutely necessary, such as creating a person label that serves as a standard when checking the reliability of the model scorer.

tabs.label: Model scoring
tabs.body: A separate model evaluates the output based on criteria, also called LLM-as-judge. It's fast, flexible, scalable, and handles complex judgments. However, if you want to trust and use it, you must first check its reliability and then expand it. First, we check whether the same value is given for the same input and how well it matches the person label.

tabs.label: Gemini Assessment Service
tabs.body: Gemini Assessment Services offers four assessment methods: Adaptive rubrics that create pass/fail checks for each prompt, static rubrics that apply the same criteria to all prompts, calculation-based metrics that use deterministic algorithms like ROUGE or BLEU, and user-defined functions that define your own Python logic. Calculation-based indicators are used when there is a correct answer, and rubric-based indicators are suitable for tasks that are difficult to evaluate with an algorithm, such as writing quality or following directions.

screens.outro: Now let's grade the same answer using multiple grading methods.

screens.title: Grading the same answer with code and model
screens.lead: Click the Next button to see step-by-step how different raters judge one answer differently.

visual.alt: An illustration of one answer going through three graders and receiving different scoring values.
labels: Standard answer: Refund possible within 14 days

steps.title: Answers and Standard Answers
steps.body: The model's answer is "Refunds are possible within 14 days" and the standard answer is "Refunds are possible within 14 days." To a person, it means the same thing, but the letters are not the same. This minor difference can lead to different results depending on the scoring method.

steps.title: Like eq of string_check
steps.body: `eq` gives 1 only when the input is exactly the same as the reference, so this answer is 0. `like` checks whether the input contains a reference string, but since the standard answer is not contained as a sentence, the result may be different from what is expected. Rule-based comparisons discount normal answers even if the wording is slightly different.

steps.title: text_similarity
steps.body: Indicators such as `fuzzy_match`, `bleu`, and `rouge` give a value ranging from 0 to 1 to indicate how similar it is to the reference. Even if the expressions are different, the larger the overlap, the higher the score. However, if the word order or vocabulary is significantly different, even if the meaning is the same, it may be expressed low.

steps.title: score_model
steps.body: The screening model returns a value within a defined range based on the criteria specified in the prompt. In the above example, a high value can be given because it is read and determined whether the meaning is the same. If the output is not a number, it is treated as 0, so only numbers should be written in the rubric.

steps.title: price of rigor
steps.body: Strict string comparisons truncate normal answers even if the meaning is the same. For example, `1` and `1.0` are treated as different values ​​in function arguments. In this case, supplementing with similarity or model scoring can reduce answers that are unfairly discounted.

screens.outro: To use model scoring, you need to use a good rubric. We'll see how in the next screen.

screens.title: Grading rubrics and grading bias
screens.lead: Each selection unfolds principles for designing a model scorer. Check them out one by one.

items.prompt: How specific should the rubric be?
items.answer: Be detailed and clear. For example, if you write something like “The product name must be included in the first sentence of the answer, and if it is not included, it is automatically judged as inappropriate,” the decision result will not be swayed. Ambiguous criteria are read differently by each grader.

items.prompt: How do I determine the output format of the grader?
items.answer: Be empirical and specific, such as only outputting “fit” or “misfit,” or limiting it to a scale of 1 to 5. Purely descriptive assessments are difficult to conduct quickly and at scale.

items.prompt: What would be better if we let the screening model infer first?
items.answer: Turning on Thinking to have the judging model make inferences before making decisions will improve evaluation performance on complex judgments. If the reason for the decision remains, it is easy to check for misjudgments later.

items.prompt: What biases should we check for?
items.answer: We check the length, tone of voice, answer order, and tendency to prefer answers written by models of the same class as the review model. You can tell if there is bias by creating pairs with the same content but different in just one characteristic and looking at the difference in scoring values.

items.prompt: When can we start trusting model graders?
items.answer: Since the scorer is also a model, we first re-examine how well it matches the human-scored labels and scale up to a larger scale when we feel confident enough. Even after magnification, it is safe to occasionally take samples and compare them to human labels.

screens.outro: Now, let's use an example to explain the bias in model scoring that favors long answers.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Model Scoring Bias in Favoring Long Answers
screens.lead: The instructor explains a hypothetical case. Click the Next button to follow along as we identify and reduce bias.

steps.title: symptoms
steps.body: The evaluation model gives higher scores to long answers with a lot of unnecessary information than to short answers with the same content. The team didn't notice that the model was becoming increasingly verbose, so they tried to adopt a change because the value had gone up.

steps.title: cause
steps.body: There was no guidance on length in the rubric. This makes it easier for the screening model to read answers that appear detailed as better answers. The model scorer is also a model, so it is affected by these appearances.

steps.title: check
steps.body: Create pairs of answers with the same content but different lengths to see the difference in scoring. If the differences are consistently towards length, then length bias is confirmed. This check can also be done as part of an evaluation set.

steps.title: Response 1: Enhancing the rubric
steps.body: Add “Points will be deducted for unnecessary repetition and redundancy” in the rubric. And clearly write down what you are evaluating, such as “Only the accuracy and completeness of the content are evaluated.”

steps.title: Response 2: Parallel scoring of rules
steps.body: It is more accurate to check the upper length limit with code. By combining model scoring and code scoring, they can cover each other's weaknesses. Conversely, including length as a criterion for a good answer solidifies bias as the standard.

steps.title: recheck
steps.body: After reinforcement, the degree of agreement with the human label is measured again. If the bias has been reduced, the difference in scores should be smaller for pairs of different lengths. Only after this verification is the scorer used for large-scale evaluation.

screens.outro: This time, we will look at an example of choosing a grading method based on the type of task.

screens.title: Case Study: Choosing Grading Methods for Different Types of Tasks
screens.lead: The instructor selects the appropriate grading method for each of the four tasks. Click the next button to check the basis for your decision.

steps.title: principles
steps.body: The scoring method picks the fastest, most reliable, and most scalable. For tasks that can be judged by rules, code scoring is the top priority, and model scoring is added only to parts that are difficult to write with rules.

steps.title: Task A: Check classification labels
steps.body: Code scoring such as exact match is the fastest and most reliable because you only need to see if the printed label matches the expected label. There is no reason to use model scoring.

steps.title: Task B: JSON fields and tool call arguments
steps.body: Field values or arguments in tool calls are compared as `string_check`. However, minor differences in format, such as `1` and `1.0`, are compensated for by similarity or model scoring to prevent normal answers from being discounted.

steps.title: Task C: Open-ended summary
steps.body: The code checks whether required items are included and whether the length upper limit is adhered to. Realism and tone are left to scoring the model with a scoring rubric. Reporting the two results separately will help you determine which one is the problem.

steps.title: Multiple results into one
steps.body: When combining scorers, you can create a single value by weighting them like the `multi` scorer. A common example is a configuration where the function name and arguments are scored separately and then combined by 0.5. The weight is determined by the cost of failure. No matter which method you choose, comparison is only possible if you measure before and after the change using the same evaluation set and the same grader.

screens.outro: Lastly, let me summarize the main points.

screens.title: Key theorems and connections
screens.lead: We summarize the selection criteria for the three scoring methods. Read slowly and think of my grader.

paragraphs: Code grading is fast, reliable, and can run at scale, but it's weak at making nuanced judgments. Model scoring is flexible and handles complex judgments, but requires specific rubrics and reliability checks. Human grading is high quality, but slow and expensive, so it is only used where absolutely necessary.

Model scorers can focus on features that are irrelevant to the content, such as length. So we check the bias separately, measure the consistency with the human label, and then zoom in. Grading methods are chosen according to the assignment and combined if necessary.

Going back to the starting question for this lesson, the slowness and shakiness of human grading can be significantly reduced by a combination of leaving the rules to the code and the judgment to a model with a rubric. However, automation does not equal accuracy, so two checks should be part of the scoring system: consistency with human labels and bias checks.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Grading is also a system. As the evaluation target is improved, the grader must also be inspected and improved. If you change scorers, you will also need to re-measure your baseline as you cannot directly compare your previous results.

checks.intro: Consider an example of bias in model scoring. Just choose the most appropriate inspection and response.
checks.q: The evaluation model has the same content, but gives higher ratings to long answers with a lot of redundancy. What is the most appropriate way to identify and reduce this bias?
options: Increase the temperature of the evaluation model to diversify evaluation
Change the standard so that longer answers are better.
Create pairs with the same content but different lengths to see the differences, add repetitive deductions to the standard, and rule grading for the upper length limit.
Bias is the essence of model scoring, so we only switch to human scoring
checks.explain: Length bias can be identified by measuring the difference in evaluations of pairs with the same content but different lengths. Unnecessary repetition deductions are added to the rubric, length restrictions are implemented through codes, and consistency with human labels is measured again.

wrong.0: Increasing the temperature only makes the ratings more shaky and does not eliminate the bias.
wrong.1: This is a direction that solidifies bias as a standard.
wrong.3: Human scoring is slow and expensive, so it is used to a minimum, and model scoring can be used for checking and supplementation.

checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. We identified the bias in pairs and pointed out the flow of complementing it with rubrics and scoring rules.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Bias is something that needs to be identified and reduced. Look again for options that include both confirmation and supplementation methods.

glossary.def: This is a method of determining whether output matches using rules and codes. The fastest and most reliable.
This is where a separate model evaluates the output based on criteria.
This is a guideline that describes the basis for giving the scoring value for each item. It is written on a specific and empirical scale.
This is the tendency for graders to bias values based on characteristics unrelated to the content, such as length.
This is a value between 0 and 1 that indicates the degree to which a part of the answer was correct.

misconceptions.myth: Model scoring completely replaces human scoring.
misconceptions.fact: Since the model scorer is also a model, it must first check the degree of agreement with the human label. People labels will continue to be needed as a basis for that.

misconceptions.myth: Code grading is simple and therefore of little use.
misconceptions.fact: It's the fastest, most reliable, and #1 choice for many tasks. Model scoring is added only to areas that cannot be covered by rules.

misconceptions.myth: A long and detailed answer is a good answer.
misconceptions.fact: Length can cause bias in model scoring. Check the length separately and, if necessary, use the upper limit in parallel as a rule.

closing.lead: The key points of this class are summarized as follows.
points: The grading method is chosen according to the assignment.
The strengths of code scoring are speed and reliability, and the strengths of model scoring are flexibility.
Rubrics are written as concrete, empirical scales.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for you to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What characteristics does our grader implicitly like, such as length or tone of voice?
